job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Sam Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good to meet you. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Whatever you say is confidential, so give me the public answer and the private one if they differ. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in the second half of a master's in mechanical engineering, focused on heating and cooling systems for buildings. I'm up at seven, in the lab by nine, and I spend most afternoons on a heat pump test rig that keeps tripping its breaker. I rent a room in student housing in Dunmore. My dad's a plumber with a bad back, and I'd rather be on a job site than in a seminar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, nothing to see. Every few years there's a new thing that's going to change everything, and the boiler still needs bleeding. I'd keep working and say nothing online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the best case for me because building services is mostly hands-on work, but it doesn't fix my money. I've got a loan the size of a small car and almost nothing saved. Not many firms near Dunmore hire graduate engineers, maybe three or four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, then send applications to every building services firm in a two-hour drive. I'd phone the people I met at my internships, Harcourt Heating and a firm called Penn & Rowe, instead of emailing. If I'm honest I'd also ask my dad whether his old customers know anyone hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. Not calm, but okay. I get a bit knotted up thinking about the loan, but a plateau means I know the rules and can work with them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd rather be on a job site. Would a plateau make that easier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd take any job, even as a service engineer fitting heat pumps, and work up. I'd rather get paid to learn on site than wait for a graduate scheme. My dad would say it's not beneath me, and he'd be right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's your plan if no firm calls back by summer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I've never used one for anything. It's not a principle, I just haven't needed it, and I'd rather work out a pipe sizing myself than trust something I can't check. If a firm needed me to, I'd learn, but slowly.

I'd keep my head down and **keep working**.

feel: **Okay but not calm**, because the loan still knots my stomach.

fieldNote: Hands-on bias makes plateau comfortable, yet **debt** keeps him anxious.

Resistant to AI tools out of habit, not principle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office side is going to go first. People I know in software are nervous, and I'm glad I'm in a trade that needs a person with a spanner. I'd keep my head down and not gloat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a mixed picture. Design, load calculations and drawings, that's thinking work, and software will take a lot of it. Somebody still has to install the thing, commission it and fix it when it fails. So my side of the job gets bigger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd aim for commissioning and service roles, which are mostly on site, and learn the controls software that comes with heat pumps. I'd take one evening course on building energy models, because the design side is changing. And I'd still not touch generative tools until a firm asks me to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little restless. I'm not scared the way I'd be if I were a coder, but the entry-level desk jobs are shrinking, and I need one to get a start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of your own work do you think software takes in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Drawing updates, the heat-loss sums and the paperwork for building regulations. At Penn & Rowe, the junior did those all day. A software package did the same in minutes by the time I left, so firms will want fewer juniors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd been slow with AI tools. Does that change here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. If the firm says do it, I'll do it. But I'd learn it by taking a real job and having someone show me, not from a course. That's how I learn everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people in charge are asleep. I'd tell people to look after their families and learn a skill that needs hands. I'd say it at the pub, not online, because I can't stand the arguing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's rough. Heat-loss sums, drawings and design go by 2028, and I'm the sort of person who gets hired for that first. Robots take three more years to reach the site, which gives me a bit of runway, but I've a loan and no safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd drop the master's thesis polish and get a job fitting heat pumps with Harcourt Heating, even if it's a trainee wage. I'd learn the trade properly from the older fitters. I'd save every pound and avoid anything on credit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and a bit angry. I'm not the sort who panics, but I wouldn't sleep well. I'd go for long walks on the moor to think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years. What do you think happens to a student with a loan like yours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say get under a house and learn something that doesn't need a screen. He's been saying that since I picked engineering. He'd probably be right this time, though he'd never say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your dad react to it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm not sure how my dad, a plumber with a bad back, copes when the robots reach his job by 2031. That's the bit I'd keep from him for now.

feel: **Anxious and angry**, with poor sleep and long walks to think.
S2.quote: I'm not sure how my dad, a plumber with a bad back, copes when the robots reach his job by 2031.
fieldNote: The hands-on trade offers a few extra years, but he worries about his **father**.
Chooses a practical fallback: fitting, not more study.
Keeps his fear private and avoids online arguments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say take it seriously but don't panic. Five years is plenty of time to learn a skill that lasts. I'd tell my mates on the course to get site experience, not just a degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel less jumpy. I'd have a job by next year, some of the loan paid and a trade under my belt by 2031. The thinking side of my job goes, but I'd be good at the installing side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get a graduate job in building services and push for site time every week. I'd pay down the loan with a third of each pay cheque. And in my third year I'd start studying for a chartered qualification, since the site experience counts toward it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady. It's not nice, but it's something I can plan around. I'd feel more like a bloke with a to-do list than a bloke with a storm on the way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years instead of two. What changes about how you'd use the time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a few years, probably. Robots that can do what my dad does are a long way from fitting a boiler in a damp cellar. But I'd not bet my life on it, so I'd pick up the controls and software side too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think the hands-on side is really safe for those three extra years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be doing the real job, just with more screens. I'd probably start using the AI tools by then, because the firm would hand me one. I'd just double-check it, the way I check a pipe size.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, so just get on with it. I'd tell the lads to learn something with a trade in it and not waste the decade complaining. I'd also say governments should think about people like my dad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I feel fine. I'd have a decade on site and in design, a smaller loan and maybe a house. The thinking side will change a lot, but I'll have made myself the guy who can do both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a graduate job, clear the loan by about thirty, and keep building on site skills. I'd save for a deposit on a flat near Dunmore. And I'd probably start learning to program control systems, because that's where building services goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly good. There's no rush, which is the best thing. I'd still worry about my dad's back and about whether he'll have a pension that covers a decent retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, would you move toward the bigger changes or wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Move toward it, slowly. I'd do the course for energy models, learn the new controls and maybe use an AI tool for the drafting. Not first, but not last either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you like to have by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A flat, no debt and a job I'd be proud of. And my dad retired with enough money that he doesn't need to climb under another house.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd have no time and a loan. What would help is a job placement on site, and some kind of loan pause. I'd also want my dad's pension protected.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how I'd feel about being a bloke who doesn't use the new tools. I don't think I'm better than people who do. I'd just like to learn something because I need it, not because I'm scared of being left behind.

headlineQuote: I'd just like to learn something because I need it, not because I'm scared of being left behind.
portrait: Sam is a **24-year-old** top mechanical engineering graduate doing a master's in building heating and cooling, living in student housing in Dunmore.
He carries a **heavy loan** and has almost no savings; his dad is a plumber with a bad back.
He's pragmatic, centre in politics, and **never uses AI tools**, preferring to learn on real jobs.
He feels safest when work is on site, so his mood stays **anxious** until ten years give him room.
He plans to take any practical job first and keeps his fears about his father private.
biggestWorry: The **two-year scenario**, because it leaves no time and he still has the loan.
whatWouldHelp: A **site-based job placement**, a loan pause and a protected pension for his dad.
